caption:
Why is Halley's Comet on the Bayeux Tapestry?

The tapestry is not a tapestry. It is embroidery — coloured wool stitched onto linen, 68.38 metres long and half a metre tall, nine panels sewn together after each was worked. Scholars think it was made in England in the 1070s, probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother, and probably stitched by women needleworkers.

In scene 32, men point up at a star with a streaming tail while Harold sits newly crowned. Below him, in the border, a fleet of ghostly ships. It is the first known picture of Halley's Comet. The same cloth also carries the earliest known depiction of a harrow.

The arrow in Harold's eye may not be original. Engravings made in 1729 and 1730 show a spear or lance there instead, with no fletchings, and needle holes in the linen suggest something was removed and fletchings added later. Medieval iconography held that a perjurer died with a weapon through the eye — which suits a story built to argue that Harold broke his oath.

Still unresolved: who designed it, whether Harold died by arrow or sword, what the oath actually promised, and what the missing end panels showed. A poem by Baldric of Dol describes a similar hanging ending with William's coronation in London.

The tapestry was confiscated in 1792 to cover military wagons and rescued by a local lawyer. In 1944 the Gestapo moved it to the Louvre; Himmler's order to send it onward was intercepted at Bletchley Park.

Images: photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry by Myrabella; scene 1 photographed by the Université de Caen Normandie campaign, 2017; engraving by Charles Alfred Stothard, 1823. All public domain.

cards.headline: The <y>first picture of Halley's Comet</y> is stitched in wool
cards.note: Scene 32 of the Bayeux Tapestry. Men point at a star with a streaming tail above a newly crowned Harold.
cards.alt: Embroidered men pointing up at a comet with a streaming tail above towers.

cards.headline: Not a tapestry at all — <y>wool stitched onto linen</y>
cards.note: 68.38 metres long, half a metre tall. Nine linen panels, each embroidered, then sewn together.
cards.source: Bayeux Tapestry, scene 1 · Université de Caen Normandie
cards.alt: Embroidered scene of King Edward seated, labelled EDWARD REX above an arch.

cards.headline: The oath is named — <y>but never explained</y>
cards.note: The Latin says Harold swore to Duke William on holy relics. Nothing on the cloth says what he promised.
cards.alt: Harold reaching toward two reliquaries under Latin lettering about an oath.

cards.headline: It credits the coronation to an <y>excommunicated archbishop</y>
cards.note: Stigand is named beside the crowned Harold. Scholars now think Ealdred of York actually performed it.
cards.alt: Crowned Harold enthroned with orb and sceptre beside a robed archbishop.

cards.headline: Drawings from the 1720s show a <y>spear, not an arrow</y>
cards.note: Engravings of 1729 and 1730 show no fletchings. Needle holes suggest something was removed and altered.
cards.alt: Coloured 1823 engraving of tapestry scenes with ships, horses and Latin text.

cards.headline: The comet is real. <y>Harold's death is not settled.</y>
cards.note: "Harold" sits above several figures — one struck in the eye, one cut down by a sword. How he died is still debated.
cards.alt: Battle scene with mounted knight, falling soldier and Latin words about Harold slain.
